result.markdown: --- title: N-Mixture Model and More title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: ../img/fish_back.jpg format: revealjs: chalkboard: true multiplex: true --- ## Objectives - N-mixture model - Occurrence Probability and Abundance - Integrated Data Modeling ## A new model {.scrollable} - [Royle 2004](https://academic.oup.com/biometrics/article/60/1/108/7289296) - [Bayesian Analysis of Spatially Structured Population Dynamics](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-031-64518-1) - Another way to estimate abundance with imperfect detection - mark recapture - removal sampling - distance sampling - double observer ## N-mixture model - Fundamentally a 'count model' that corrects for detection probability ::: {.incremental} - "Capture–recapture studies can be difficult to implement" (Royle, 2004) - Maybe more useful for sparse data (few sites, few occasions, small detection probability, some zeros) - **Data Inputs**: Replicated spatial counts - **Abundance**: State process is a Poisson distribution - **Detection**: Observation process is a Binomial distribution ::: ## N-mixture model {.scrollable} $y_{i,t}$ = number of individuals observed at site $i=1...R$ during $t=1...T$ sampling occasions. . . . $$ \begin{align*} y_{i,t} \sim& \text{Binomial}(N_i, p) \\ N_i \sim& \text{Poisson}(\lambda) \end{align*} $$ . . . - $N_i$ = size of population at site $i$ - $\sum_{i=1}^R N_i$ = total population size . . . **Priors:** - $\text{log}(\lambda) \sim \text{Normal}(0,3)$ - OR, $\lambda \sim \text{Gamma}(0.01,0.01)$ - $\text{logit}(p) \sim \text{Logistic}(0,1)$ - OR, $p \sim \text{Beta}(1,1)$ ## N Mixture Model **Assumptions:** 1) Poisson and binomial distributions are true descriptions of state and observation processes; i.e., variation in abundance can be described by the assumed distribution (e.g., Poisson). :::{.incremental} 2) Abundance at each site $i$ is random and independent of abundance at all other sites; 3) Population is closed among surveys 4) Observers do not double count individuals 5) All individuals have the same detection probability or otherwise modeled ::: ## Data ![](../img/data.nmixture.png){fig-align="center" width="300"} ## N-mixture extensions $y_{i,t}$ = number of individuals observed at site $i=1...R$ during $t=1...T$ sampling occasions. $$ \begin{align*} y_{i,t} \sim& \text{Binomial}(N_i, p_{i,t}) \\ N_i \sim& \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i) \end{align*} $$ . . . $$ \begin{align*} \text{logit}(p_{i,t}) =& \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times x_{i,t} \\ \text{log}(\lambda_{i}) =& \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \times w_{i} + \epsilon_{i} \\ \epsilon_{i} \sim& \text{Normal}(0,\sigma^2) \end{align*} $$ ## More extensions - Other distributions - Negative-binomial - Zero-inflated Poisson - Multinomial - Integrate known date or distance information - Multiple states, ages, or sexes - Spatial movement, e.g., temporary emigration ## Implementation - Maximum likelihood - Unmarked pacakge; pcount function - Bayesian - ubms package - JAGS, nimble, INLA, stan ## Concerns **Parameter Identifiability**: "A model is identifiable if there is only one set of parameter values that result in a single model output". [(Cole book)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13253-021-00441-7) . . . **Data Identifiability**: a condition of the unique dataset that does not allow the model to estimate a unique set of parameters to be output . . . ![](../img/cole table.png){fig-align="center" width="700"} ## Concerns [Link et al. 2018](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ecy.2362) [Barker et al. 2017](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/biom.12734) - 2% double counting can lead to ~20% bias ::: {.incremental} - small unmodelled heterogenity in $p$ can lead to 20% bias - small distributional assumption violation leads to CI coverage of 17% ::: ## Concerns [Link et al. 2018](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ecy.2362) [Barker et al. 2017](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/biom.12734) - "fundamentally count data under imperfect detection can only be reliably used as indices." (i.e., relative abundance, not absolute abundance) . . . ... this is because without auxiliary information about $p$, count data cannot distinguish between an N-mixture model and other possible models (GLM). ## Concerns [Kery, 2017 ](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1002/ecy.2093) - Testing concern with 137 bird datasets - Small sample size caused issues (<267 sites) - Covariates did not affect identifiabiltiy - No identifiability issues for Poisson and ZIP distributional assumptions - 25% of datasets had issues with Negative Binomial distribution ## N-mixture model Go to code.... ![](../img/jags.n.mixture.png){fig-align="center" width="300"} ## Occurrence Probability and Expected Abundance {.scrollable} $\psi$ = probability of occurrence $\lambda$ = mean count/abundance . . . $$ \psi = P(Y=1) $$ . . . $$ \psi = P(Y=1) = P(N>0) $$ . . . $$ \psi = P(Y=1) = P(N>0) = 1 - e^{-\lambda} $$ . . . ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lambda = 2 psi = 1 - exp(-lambda) psi ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.8646647 ``` ::: ::: . . . The Probability of observing > 0 counts, given lambda = 2 ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ppois(0,lambda=2,lower.tail = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.8646647 ``` ::: ::: ## More to the idea {.scrollable} **Starting with:** $$ \psi = 1 - e^{-\lambda} $$ . . . **Lets rearrange:** $$ e^{-\lambda} = 1 - \psi $$ . . . $$ \text{log}(e^{-\lambda}) = \text{log}(1 - \psi) $$ . . . $$ -\lambda = \text{log}(1 - \psi) $$ . . . $$ \lambda = -\text{log}(1 - \psi) $$ . . . $$ \text{log}(\lambda) = \text{log}(-\text{log}(1 - \psi)) $$ . . . The right side is called the 'complimentary log-log link function'. ## The end result {.scrollable} $$ \text{log}(\lambda) = \text{log}(-\text{log}(1 - \psi)) $$ OR $$ \text{log}(-\text{log}(1 - \psi)) = \text{log}(\lambda) $$ . . . OR $$ \text{cloglog}(\psi) = \text{log}(\lambda) $$ . . . OR $$ \text{cloglog}(\psi) = \text{log}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \times x_1) $$ ## The model all together {.scrollable} $y_i$ are the presence and absences of the species at site $i$... $$ y_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\psi_i) \\ \text{cloglog}(\psi_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times x_i $$ ## Presence/Absence Model Go to code.... ![](../img/jags.cloglog.png){fig-align="center" width="300"} ## Integrated Data Model - a hierarchical model ::: {.incremental} - separate response variables where at least one parameter is shared among at least 2 response variables - "It just makes sense to use all the information that is available in some estimation task" (Kery and Kellner, 2024) ::: ## Integrated Data Model - **Names**: integrated model, data fusion, data assimilation - specific types: - integrated population models - integrated species distribution models - integrated community model - integrate dynamic N-mixture model ## Integrated Data Model "datastream specific observation submodels that inform a common ecological model” [Gilbert et al. 2021](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0006320721001993) ## Integrated Species Distribution Model In chapter 20 of Kery and Kellner, 2024 they introduce three data sets. 1. Counts of swifts ($y_1$) 2. Counts of swifts, but the "lazy" birdwatchers didn't record the zero counts ($y_2$) 3. Observers recorded whether swifts were present (1) or not (0) ($y_3$) ## Integrated Species Distribution Model We could fit each separately, but... . . . Or, could fit a model that leverages all three data sets, each with their own observation model but a single joint 'process/state' model. ## Integrated Data Model {.scrollable} #### Sub model 1 $$ \begin{align*} y_{1,i} \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda) \end{align*} $$ #### Sub model 2 $$ \begin{align*} y_{2,i} \sim \text{ZT Poisson}(\lambda) \end{align*} $$ #### Sub model 3 $$ \begin{align*} y_{3,i} \sim \text{Binomial}(\psi) \end{align*} $$ ## Integrated Data Model {.scrollable} #### Sub model 1 $$ \begin{align*} y_{1,i} \sim& \text{Poisson}(\lambda_{i}) \\ \text{log}(\lambda_{i}) =& \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times x_i \end{align*} $$ ::: {.fragment} #### Sub model 2 $$ \begin{align*} y_{2,i} \sim& \text{ZT Poisson}(\lambda_i)\\ \text{log}(\lambda_{i}) =& \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times x_i \end{align*} $$ ::: ::: {.fragment} #### Sub model 3 $$ \begin{align*} y_{3,i} \sim& \text{Binomial}(\psi_{i})\\ \text{cloglog}(\psi) =& \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times x_i \end{align*} $$ ::: ## Integrated Data Model Go to code... ![](../img/jags.im.model.png){fig-align="center" width="300"}
